tagline: A paved climb from Wells into the ice-carved East Humboldt Range
intro: Angel Lake Road climbs from Wells into the East Humboldt Range, a 12-mile paved drive through switchbacks to a glacial lake. U-shaped canyons, moraines and granite cliffs show the work of past glaciers along the way. Designated a Nevada Scenic Byway in 1995, the road reaches what the Forest Service calls the area’s only alpine lake accessible by pavement. The range has a steep eastern escarpment and gentler slopes to the west, the result of its tilted fault-block formation.
The lake takes its name from Warren M. Angel, an early rancher in Clover Valley. The road became a state highway on July 1, 1976, before receiving its scenic designation on June 30, 1995.

Starting at Humboldt Avenue in Wells, just south of I-80, follow Angel Lake Road toward the mountains and their eastern switchbacks. The state highway ends at the Angel Lake fee booth, beside the lake’s picnic and campground areas. At the lake, high cliffs enclose the basin, with Greys Peak to the west and Chimney Rock’s pinnacles to the south. Clover Valley and Wells lie below to the east.
notice: U-shaped canyons, moraines and granite cliffs are visible from the road.

moments.title: Wells
moments.text: Before the mountain drive, Wells offers another kind of travel history: a California-trail stopping place that became a railroad town. Its original name, Humboldt Wells, refers to springs and swampy ground west of the city where the Humboldt River begins. During an 1877 fire, a telegraph message called for help: “Wells is burning”. The rebuilt town used the shorter name. The original Transcontinental Railroad once brought passenger trains here; Wells now stands at the junction of I-80 and US 93. The city stands at an elevation of 5,630 feet.

moments.title: The switchbacks
moments.text: The road’s switchbacks climb the steep eastern side of the East Humboldt Range. The range formed as a tilted fault block, with more gradual slopes and valleys on its western side. Glaciers later left U-shaped canyons, moraines, granite cliffs and cirques, all visible from the road to Angel Lake. Greys Peak reaches 10,674 feet near the northern end of the range; farther south, the mountains rise higher at Hole in the Mountain Peak. Clover Valley borders the mountains to the east, while Starr Valley and Dennis Flats lie on their western side.
moments.notice: The mountain road reveals U-shaped canyons and steep granite cliffs.

moments.title: Angel Lake
moments.text: Angel Lake occupies a glacial basin at 8,378 feet in the northern East Humboldt Range. Its approximately 13 acres sit beneath high cirque cliffs, with the pinnacles of Chimney Rock to the south. The lake reaches a depth of up to 29 feet beneath those enclosing cliffs. The lake bears the name of Warren M. Angel, an early Clover Valley rancher. The Forest Service describes a lakeshore picnic area and a campground beside the lake, flanked by glacial cirques. The Forest Service lists both facilities as closed for the season.
moments.notice: High cliffs enclose the lake, with Chimney Rock’s pinnacles to the south.
